SELF Turing Machine There exists a Turing machine named SELF that can generate its own code without any external input. For details on SELF, refer to Chapter 6 (first few pages) of the Theory of Computation book by Sipser.
SELF is composed of two parts, A, B both Turing machines. First, A runs and leaves <B>, the description of TM B, on the tape. Then, B runs and analyses the contents of the tape to determine the description <A> of the Turing machine that left the contents on the tape. Finally, B combines the descriptions <A> and <B> to create a new description of SELF, denoted as <AB>.
We consider A and B as functions in the following code: We model the tape used by A,B with a global variable s.
First, we create function A(), which simply writes the description <B> into string s. We use a placeholder for now, until we write function B(). Once that’s done, we can copy and paste the code as a string (without the indentation) into s.
Next, we create the code for B(). This function needs to print function A() followed by function B(). To achieve this, we need two print statements. The first print statement prints part of function A(), and the value of s in the last line of A() is printed from s itself. The second print statement prints the code for function B(), which is in string s itself.
We will write the code in two steps. In the first step, we will print s without the surrounding single quotes, and in the second step, we will add the single quotes.
The indentation will still not be right. It would be an interesting exercise for the reader to fix the indentation. Ideally, the code that is printed should run without any reformatting.
Stage 1. The complete Turing machine is located in the first cell. The tape is represented by a global variable called ’s’. Two functions, A() and B(), are used in the construction of SELF as described in the book. Note that we have to write the code for B first, then populate the hand side of s= in function A. The SELF machine can be executed by calling A and then B.the right
global s # we will use s as the tape. # A will print <B> onto s def A(): global s s = 'def B(): global s print("def A(): global s s =", s) print(s)' # B will use q(<B>) to print description of A # and combine <A> with <B> to print self def B(): global s print("global s def A(): global s s =", s) # prints A() print(s) # prints B() # prints the code more or less - there are two issues # 1. missing when s = '' # 2. new line characters are missing # see if you fix these A() B() global s def A(): global s s = def B(): global s print("def A(): global s s =", s) print(s) def B(): global s print("def A(): global s s =", s) print(s) Stage 2: The first line prints the contents of s without quotes. As a first attempt, one could try to print ' in first print in B, but this requires escaping the quotes using \. A bit of playing around with this idea would convince you that the headache now is to print \. We need to specify the quote as a string of characters which, when printed using print, will print ' but when treated as a string is printed as a string. Single quote is also represented as chr(0x27) and this is the string we use.
A simple modification the code above: insertion of chr(0x27) before and after s is printed the first time in B does the trick. It will print s within quotes when function A is being printed. This modifies the definition of B therefore we have to update the string s in A as well.
When A,B are called one after the other then the two functions are printed as a single line. Convince yourself that the output is the same as the code in the cell (upto indentation).
print(chr(0x27)) ' chr(0x27) The code below fixes the ' issue.
global s def A(): global s s = 'def B(): global s print("global s def A(): global s s =", chr(0x27), s, chr(0x27)) print(s)' def B(): global s print("global s def A(): global s s =", chr(0x27), s, chr(0x27)) print(s) A() B() global s def A(): global s s = ' def B(): global s print("global s def A(): global s s =", chr(0x27), s, chr(0x27)) print(s) ' def B(): global s print("global s def A(): global s s =", chr(0x27), s, chr(0x27)) print(s) A good exercise to test your understanding would be to modify the program so that the indentation is also preserved. It will require some effort, though.

Biography Daya Gaur obtained B. Tech (hons) in CSE from IT-BHU, Varanasi and M.Sc. and Ph.D, degrees from School of Computing Science, Simon Fraser University. He is a Professor (Full) of Computer Science at the University of Lethbridge. His research interests are in Algorithms both classical and Quantum. He is a founding member of the https://www.ulethbridge.ca/artsci/math-computer-science/optimization-research-group[Optimization Research Group, Lethbridge], member of Quantum Alberta and Southern Alberta Genome Sciences Center.
He has held visiting appointments at STCS, TIFR Mumbai, Department of CSE, IIT Delhi, Department of CSE, IIT BHU. He served as Head, Department of Computer Science and Engineering, IIT Ropar and as Head, Department of Mathematics, IIT Ropar. He was advisor to an emerging technology startup, Inbridge Inc. His Erdős number is 2.
Research My research interests are in Combinatorial Optimization, Bioinformatics and Quantum Algorithms. The research has been supported by NSERC Canada, Department of Science and Technology, Govt. of India, Alberta Innovates (Quantum MIF) and University of Lethbridge.
Teaching I have taught a variety of courses at the undergraduate and the graduate level. I have taught courses at Simon Fraser University, University of Lethbridge, TIFR Mumbai, IIT Delhi, IIT Ropar, IIT Mandi and at IIT BHU. Some of the courses that I have taught in the recent past are listed below.
Quantum Computation, CPSC 4110, 5110, Fall 2021. Approximation Algorithms, CPSC 5110, Fall 2016, Fall 2019 Discrete Structures for Computer Science, CPSC 1820, Spring 2015, Spring 2016, Fall 2017, Fall 2018, Spring 2020 Data Structures and Algorithms CPSC 3620, Spring 2017, Fall 2017, Spring 2018, Fall 2018. Artificial Intelligence, CPSC 3750, Spring 2015 Computer Networks CPSC 3780, Fall 2014, Fall 2016 Programming Languages CPSC 3740, Spring 2016, Spring 2017, Spring 2020 Theory of Computation, CPSC 3630, Fall 2014, Fall 2019 Advanced Algorithms, CPSC 4625, Spring 2018 A select list of recent independent studies is below.
Behaviour Trees: Intro to Mult. Agent Systems, CPSC 3990, Summer 2018 Approximation Algorithms, CPSC 5990, Spring 2015, Spring 2017, Fall 2018. Approximation Algorithms, CPSC 7990, Fall 2018. Mining of Massive Data Sets, CPSC 4990, Spring 2015 Practical Bioninformatics, CPSC 3990, Summer 2016 Quantum Computation, CPSC 5990, Summer 2016 Please visit https://moodle.uleth.ca for resources related to the current course offerings.
Prospective Applicants to the Graduate Program: If you have a strong background in Computer Science and an interest in Algorithms/Bioinformatics/Quantum Computation feel free to send an email. The details of the application process are available at https://www.uleth.ca/sgs
